newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan business elated after rivals meet.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan business elated after rivals meet.

text.p: Business optimism in Nicaragua has soared following right-wing President Arnoldo Aleman's historic meeting with his left-wing Sandinista nemesis Daniel Ortega, business and political leaders said on Wednesday.

Last week's meeting and agreement to further meetings have eased fears of political instability and renewed investor interest in impoverished Nicaragua, said Gerardo Salinas, president of the Superior Council of Private Enterprise.

"The fact that the Sandinistas, who are the country's second power, are prepared to sit with the current government is a very important step towards the political stability that is demanded by foreign investors," Salinas told Reuters.

Nicaragua, an economic pariah in the 1980s when the Sandinistas governed with Soviet and Cuban backing, returned to the free market in the 1990s, but investors largely have stayed away as continued hostilities between the Sandinistas and Nicaragua's right wing led to fears of returned violence.
Ortega stubbornly had refused to recognise the legitimacy of Aleman's government, which took power on Jan. 10, saying it won by electoral fraud, and he warned of social unrest.

So when Ortega, an ex-president, entered his former offices to talk with Aleman about Nicaragua's political stability, business leaders heaved a sigh of relief and a triumphant Aleman predicted an investment boom.
"There are dozens of national and international investors who are coming since they saw Daniel Ortega and Arnoldo Aleman sit down and talk," Aleman told reporters.

Leaders of the private enterprise council COSEP on Monday announced the planned construction of five major hotels in the capital Managua, though they did not name the hotel companies involved. They also predicted a construction boom.

"This political stability is going to help greatly, because they say there's nothing more nervous than one million dollars and in Nicaragua even ten thousand dollars has been nervous," said Gabriel Solorzano, president of the state-funded Nicaraguan Development Institute.

Salinas said Nicaragua, the second-poorest country in Latin America after Haiti, must receive foreign investment if it is to develop because it lacks the internal resources needed to rebuild its shattered infrastructure.
"Why is investment going to be big here? Simply because everything remains to be done. Investors will often find no competition," Salinas said.
